title: Graded capacity fencing for spot-preference and GPU-class scoring
creator: Aisha Patel
summary: Implement a graduated capacity-fencing mechanism that prefers spot instances and lower-cost GPU classes while enforcing soft budget caps and providing deterministic fallbacks to on-demand / higher-class GPUs when necessary.
description:
Background: We currently have coarse spot-vs-on-demand routing and a simple budget guard that stops routing to spot when spend passes a threshold. Customers running high-throughput workloads see oscillations and unexpected latency regressions when spot eviction patterns coincide with budget depletion. This ticket designs and implements a graded capacity fencing strategy: instead of a binary allow/deny for spot or a single budget threshold, we assign per-customer, per-route capacity gates with levels (green/yellow/red) that modulate both spot preference and GPU-class selection.

Goals:
- Reduce bursty failovers and latency spikes caused by binary spot cutoffs.
- Favor cheaper GPU classes (e.g., A100-p4d -> A10g -> T4 equivalents) when cost-efficient while bounding latency impact.
- Enforce soft budget caps that shape routing probability rather than hard-stop, with deterministic escalation paths.
- Provide observability: per-customer gate state time series, projected burn rate, and decision logs for each routed request.

Design highlights:
1) GPU-class scoring: compute a dynamic score for each candidate backend based on (expected latency delta, per-token cost delta, current queue depth, and recent eviction probability). Score is a single numeric value; routing prefers lowest expected cost given latency SLO constraints. Score formula will be parameterized and tunable per-customer.
2) Graded gates: for each customer+route we maintain a gate state with 3 levels: GREEN (prefer spot / cheap GPU classes), YELLOW (deprioritize spot, allow degraded cheap classes with higher sampling to on-demand), RED (disallow spot; route to on-demand/higher-class only). Transitions are driven by trailing burn, projected spend over window, and eviction signals.
3) Soft budget caps: customers can set a soft cap. When projected spend approaches the cap, the gate transitions downward probabilistically: at YELLOW we apply an x% randomized fall-through to on-demand to preserve availability but reduce spend. At RED we always route to on-demand. The randomized behavior smooths spend and avoids synchronized global switches.
4) Eviction-aware adjustments: integrate spot eviction telemetry to temporarily increase gate severity for regions/GPU SKUs with high recent eviction rates. This avoids routing many requests into an unstable SKU.
5) Deterministic fallback model variants: when selecting model variants (quantized vs full precision), the decision logic will prefer a cheaper quantized variant if the gate level is GREEN or YELLOW (with sampling), but always include quick checks to ensure quality: sampled requests are evaluated for regression and steering back to higher-quality variants if quality thresholds break.

Operational controls and APIs:
- Console: gate visualization (level timeline per-customer), manual override, and estimation panel showing projected spend under current routing policy.
- Admin API: set soft_cap, hysteresis windows, sampling probabilities for YELLOW, and per-route latency SLOs.
- Logs: per-request routing decision record (timestamp, gate_level, selected_backend, score_breakdown, cost_estimate, model_variant). Stored for 30 days by default.

Trade-offs considered:
- Deterministic vs probabilistic transitions: deterministic thresholds cause synchronized shifts; randomized transitions improve stability but increase complexity of debugging decisions. We chose probabilistic fall-through because it materially reduced oscillation in the traffic simulator.
- Per-customer tunables vs global defaults: initial rollout will have conservative global defaults; large customers can opt into finer-grained controls.
- Data requirements: requires accurate per-backend eviction rates and short-window burn projections; we add a small in-memory projection engine to avoid excessive DB lookups.
acceptance_criteria: Gate state machine implemented with GREEN/YELLOW/RED transitions and configurable hysteresis windows
GPU-class scoring implemented and used during routing; scoring parameters are configurable via config store
Soft budget cap behavior: when projected spend crosses configured thresholds, routing probability adjusts according to sampling params
Eviction telemetry integrated and causes gate adjustments for unstable SKUs/regions
Deterministic fallback to on-demand for RED gates and sampling-based fallbacks for YELLOW
Per-request decision logs emitted and visible in Console for a test customer
Integration tests that simulate eviction storms and validate smooth spend curves (no >20% spike compared to baseline)
Performance: routing decision latency added <2ms p50 to the decision path under typical load
implementation_notes: Phase 1 (API+Scoring): implement scoring function and config knobs. Add unit tests for score stability.
Phase 2 (Gate state engine): build in-memory gate state per customer with persistence to KV and rollout via config flags.
Phase 3 (Eviction integration): wire spot eviction stream and feed to gate engine. Add dashboards for SKU-level eviction rates.
Phase 4 (Console+API): Console panels and admin API for overrides + opt-ins for customers.
Phase 5 (Rollout): Canary to 5% of traffic for low-risk customers, monitor objective metrics for 48h, then broaden to 50% and 100%.
